title: The Weaver's Cottage to the Gospel of Wealth: the Bobbin Boy, the Steel, and Homestead
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Dunfermline, birth over the hand loom
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The cottage half on Moodie Street survives as the Andrew Carnegie Birthplace Museum and supplies the coordinate; the research pool's own geography lens gave 56.0714, -3.463, which lands some four hundred metres north near the Abbey and High Street, and that value is rejected here in favour of the museum's own location.
stops.campa: In a rented half of a weaver's cottage at Moodie Street, William Carnegie works a damask hand loom on the ground floor while Margaret Morrison keeps the room above it. Their first son is born on the twenty-fifth of November, 1835, in a town whose whole trade is linen woven by hand, thirteen years before the power looms of Dunbarton and Glasgow finish that trade for good. The Morrison side are radicals and Chartists, cobblers and shopkeepers who argue politics across the table. He learns the loom's noise before he learns arithmetic.
suggested_refs: The weaver's cottage at Moodie Street and Priory Lane, now the Andrew Carnegie Birthplace Museum

stops.name: Dunfermline Abbey, the curriculum without a schoolroom
stops.date_confidence: the year is an ordering device only, chosen to place the boy at about eight. The scene rests on Carnegie's own Autobiography of 1920, self-report written seventy years after the fact, and is tagged as tradition rather than document. The coordinate is the Abbey's own, correcting the pool's 56.0715, -3.4629, which stacked almost exactly on the birthplace pin.
stops.campa: His uncle George Lauder walks him under the Abbey walls and shows him the name of Robert the Bruce cut in stone above the choir where the king lies. Wallace and Bannockburn come to him as household facts rather than lessons; so does Burns, learned by heart. Dunfermline was a capital of Scotland once, and the boy is told so early and often. Below the Abbey lies Pittencrieff Glen, walled and privately held, and the Morrisons, who are the town's agitators, are not admitted through its gate. Who refused them, and in what year, is nowhere written down.
suggested_refs: Dunfermline Abbey and the tomb of Robert the Bruce beneath the choir
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), ed. John C. Van Dyke, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Broomielaw, Glasgow, the borrowed passage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the PBS American Experience Carnegie timeline, which also names the ship Wiscasset and the twenty pounds borrowed to complete the fare. The vessel's name is carried by the same source and by Wikipedia; no passenger list was consulted in this pass.
stops.campa: The hand loom has been beaten by steam and William Carnegie has no work. Margaret borrows twenty pounds from a Dunfermline friend to close the gap in the fare. She will keep the family's accounts for the next thirty-eight years, and her son will not marry while she lives. On the seventeenth of May the family walks from the cottage down to the Glasgow quays and boards the Wiscasset, a sailing ship bound for New York. Andrew is twelve. His brother Thomas is five. The lender's name does not survive outside the family's own retelling.
suggested_refs: The Broomielaw emigrant quays at Glasgow, embarkation point of the Wiscasset, May 1848
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie timeline: rags to riches'

segments.name: The Bobbin Boy and the Wire

stops.name: Allegheny City, one dollar twenty a week
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia specifies September 1848 for the family's arrival in Allegheny; the pool's chronology lens gave a bare '1848' and is sharpened here. The wage of $1.20 per week for the bobbin boy is attested in both the PBS timeline and Wikipedia. The crossing of about fifty days and the inland passage by Hudson River and canal are attested only in general terms and no landing date at New York was established.
stops.campa: Fifty days of sail put the family ashore at New York, and the canals and rivers carry them west for weeks more to Allegheny City, across the water from Pittsburgh, where Margaret's sisters have already settled. The father takes work in a cotton factory and the twelve-year-old takes work in the same building as a bobbin boy, changing spools, at one dollar and twenty cents a week. He is soon moved to a cellar to fire a small boiler and dip new bobbins in oil, which he hates and does not admit hating. His schooling has ended for good.
suggested_refs: The cotton factories of Allegheny City, now Pittsburgh's North Side
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie timeline: rags to riches'

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the boy who reads the wire by ear
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the sequence, messenger in 1849 and operator within about a year, from Wikipedia; the month is unknown and defaulted. The coordinate is downtown Pittsburgh, where the Ohio Telegraph office and the Pennsylvania Railroad division office both stood within a few blocks; it is a district pin, not a surveyed address.
stops.campa: He is taken on as a messenger boy for the Ohio Telegraph Company and sets himself to memorise every firm and every face on the delivery round. In the office he learns the instrument by listening, and becomes one of the first operators in the country able to take a message straight off the sounder by ear without waiting for the paper tape. Every commercial message in Pittsburgh passes through that room, and a fourteen-year-old is taking them off the wire as they arrive. Within about a year the messenger is an operator.
suggested_refs: The Ohio Telegraph Company office, downtown Pittsburgh, 1849
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie timeline: rags to riches'

stops.name: Colonel Anderson's library, the letter signed Working Boy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The episode rests on Carnegie's Autobiography, self-report, with an editorial corroboration from the telegraph historian David Homer Bates; no copy of the newspaper letter was located in this pass and the year is an ordering device. The library's size, about four hundred volumes, is Carnegie's own figure.
stops.campa: Colonel James Anderson opens his four hundred volumes to working boys on Saturday afternoons, one book at a time, free. When the rule is read to exclude messenger boys because they are not apprenticed to a recognised trade, the messenger writes to the Pittsburgh newspaper over the signature Working Boy and argues the case in print. The rule is widened. He will pay for more than two thousand five hundred libraries in his lifetime and will name Anderson in the account of nearly every one of them. No copy of the letter has been found.
suggested_refs: Colonel James Anderson's private library at Allegheny, opened to working boys on Saturdays
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976
nps.gov, 'Carnegie Libraries: The Future Made Bright'

stops.name: Pittsburgh, Thomas Scott's own operator
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year and the appointment. The wage is given two ways in the pool, about $4 a week in one place and about $35 a month in another; both appear in reputable retellings, they do not reconcile exactly, and neither is adjudicated here. The month is unknown and defaulted. The train-order episode and Scott's nickname for him come from the Autobiography, self-report, and were not part of the verified pool.
stops.campa: Thomas A. Scott, superintendent of the Pennsylvania Railroad's western division, hires the seventeen-year-old telegrapher away from the wire company to be his own secretary and operator. Scott teaches him the railroad from the inside: schedules, tonnage, the cost of moving one ton one mile, and how a corporation borrows. One night, with Scott absent and the line blocked, the boy signs his superior's name to the train orders that clear it, an act that could have cost him the job and instead makes his career. Scott begins calling him my white-haired Scotch devil.
suggested_refs: The Pennsylvania Railroad's Pittsburgh division offices under Thomas A. Scott
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie timeline: rags to riches'
Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the first dividend cheque
stops.date_confidence: disputed on both date and shape. Wikipedia dates the Adams Express purchase to 1855 and describes $500 raised on a $600 mortgage of his mother's house; the research dossier dates it 1856 and describes ten shares. Both years circulate and neither is resolved here. The purchase itself is attested; the reading of the first dividend as a revelation about capital income is Carnegie's own later telling and is tradition, not document.
stops.campa: Scott arranges his clerk's first investment, a holding in the Adams Express Company, and Margaret mortgages the Allegheny house for six hundred dollars to raise it. The first dividend cheque arrives with a printed heading. Carnegie carries it out under the trees on a Sunday to show his friends, and tells the story of that morning for the rest of his life as the hour he understood that money works while a man sleeps. The sources do not agree on the year, 1855 or 1856, nor on whether what he bought was ten shares or five hundred dollars' worth.
suggested_refs: The Adams Express Company share certificate, Carnegie's first investment, raised on a mortgage of his mother's house
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Pittsburgh, superintendent at twenty-four
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by Wikipedia, which gives 1 December 1859 for the succession to Scott and a salary of $1,500 a year.
stops.campa: Scott moves up on the first of December 1859 and Carnegie takes the western division of the Pennsylvania Railroad at fifteen hundred dollars a year. He is twenty-four, small and foreign, and the division puts him at the centre of every industry that ships anything at all. He introduces night crews to clear wrecks off the line before morning. And he learns the railroad's own arithmetic, cost per ton per mile carried out to the decimal, which is what lets a firm price below any competitor who does not know what his own work costs him.
suggested_refs: The Pennsylvania Railroad Western Division superintendency, held 1859 to 1865
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie timeline: rags to riches'

segments.name: The War, the Oil, and the Iron Bridges

stops.name: Washington, the military telegraph
stops.date_confidence: attested in general terms. Scott's appointment over Union military railroads and telegraphs and Carnegie's presence with him in Washington are corroborated by Wikipedia and rest in detail on Carnegie's own Autobiography. The month is defaulted; the coordinate is the War Department precinct.
stops.campa: Scott is made assistant secretary of war with charge of the Union's military railroads and telegraphs, and he takes his old operator with him. Carnegie organises the telegraph service out of Washington and opens the rail line into the capital, moving troops on the schedules he learned in Pittsburgh. He is twenty-five. For four years the government buys iron and rails on a scale no private customer has approached, and he watches the orders go through. Scott, who hired him at seventeen, is now a cabinet officer.
suggested_refs: The United States Military Telegraph and the War Department telegraph office, Washington, 1861
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Toward Alexandria, the first blood of the war
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and flagged as legend. The wound and the joke about first blood come only from Carnegie's own later telling; Wikipedia presents it as his claim and joke rather than as any casualty record, and nothing in this pass corroborates it. The date is set to the day of First Bull Run, after which he is said to have helped move wounded men; the association is his own.
stops.campa: Restoring the cut line toward Alexandria, he pulls a telegraph wire that has been pinned down, and it whips up and lays his cheek open. He tells the story for the rest of his life as the first blood shed for the country in the Civil War, which it is not, and he tells it as a joke, which does not stop the anecdote hardening into biography. No casualty record carries it; the source is his own book, written fifty years afterwards. After Bull Run he works the trains bringing wounded men back over the line he has just repaired, in July heat, for as long as the trains keep coming.
suggested_refs: The Alexandria rail and telegraph line, repaired July 1861
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Venango County, the oil that pays a million
stops.date_confidence: contested inside the pool. Wikipedia names the vehicle as the Columbia Oil Company, Venango County, 1864; the pool's geography lens instead gave 1861-1864 and placed it at Storey Farm on Oil Creek near Titusville, which is in Crawford County. Storey Farm is the property, Columbia Oil the company, and the coordinate here sits on Oil Creek between the two readings. The figure of roughly a million dollars in a single year is Carnegie's own, from the Autobiography, and is not independently verified.
stops.campa: The first American oil rush is running up Oil Creek, and Carnegie and a group of Pittsburgh partners buy into it. The wells pay on a scale nothing in his experience has prepared him for, by his own account near a million dollars in one year at the peak; the figure is his alone and no account book confirms it. The men on the ground dig a great pond to hold the oil they cannot ship, expecting the field to run dry within a season and the price to soar. The field does not run dry. He is twenty-nine.
suggested_refs: The Columbia Oil Company and the Storey Farm property on Oil Creek, western Pennsylvania
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), ed. John C. Van Dyke, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Lawrenceville, the Keystone Bridge Company
stops.date_confidence: the date is corrected against the pool, which twice gave 1863 for Keystone. Wikipedia's Keystone Bridge Company article gives a founding of 1865; Piper and Schiffler, the partnership Carnegie helped organise, dates from about 1862 and is reorganised as Keystone in 1865. Carnegie's resignation from the Pennsylvania Railroad in 1865 is separately attested. The plant footprint is approximate.
stops.campa: Every railroad bridge in the country is made of wood and every one of them burns. Carnegie organises the men who can build them out of iron instead, first as Piper and Schiffler and from 1865 as the Keystone Bridge Company. In the same year he resigns from the Pennsylvania Railroad; his outside income passed his salary some time before, though the date it did so is not recorded. He now manufactures bridges for railroads and also sells the bonds that pay railroads for bridges. Nobody at the time calls this a conflict.
suggested_refs: The Keystone Bridge Company works at Lawrenceville, Pittsburgh
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: St. Louis, the Eads Bridge across the Mississippi
stops.date_confidence: the bridge's completion in 1874 is attested; the coordinate is corrected to the bridge itself from the pool's value, which sat over a kilometre west on the Missouri bank. Nothing in this pass places Carnegie on the bridge in person. The stop stands for the object his company built and whose bonds he sold, not for a visit; the later habit of folding it into a story that Carnegie invented steel is flagged by the source itself.
stops.campa: James Buchanan Eads throws three ribbed arches across the Mississippi at St. Louis, the first bridge of consequence to use steel in its structure, and Keystone has the ironwork. Carnegie sells the bonds that pay for it, working the London market, where the money for American railroads actually lives. He is thirty-eight and has learned to stand at both ends of the same trade, the mill that makes the metal and the banker abroad who lends against it. Nothing places him at the opening. To satisfy the doubters that the span will hold, they walk an elephant across it.
suggested_refs: The Eads Bridge at St. Louis, ironwork by the Keystone Bridge Company, completed 1874

segments.name: New York, the Memorandum, and the Steel

stops.name: St. Nicholas Hotel, the memorandum to himself
stops.date_confidence: attested. The memorandum's text is reproduced in Carnegie's own Autobiography at footnote 30 and discussed in the standard biographies by Wall and Nasaw; the exact day within December 1868 is not given and is defaulted. The 1867 move to New York, the Broad Street office and the lodging with his mother at this hotel rest on the Autobiography alone and were not independently reverified. What is not in dispute is that he did not do it: he retires at sixty-five, not thirty-five.
stops.campa: He has moved to New York, where the men who buy railroad bonds live, taken an office on Broad Street and lodgings at this hotel with his mother. He is thirty-three and worth more than most men will see. Alone in the room he writes himself a plan on a sheet of paper: cap the income at fifty thousand dollars a year, give away everything above it, quit business entirely at thirty-five, settle at Oxford, get an education, take up public affairs and writing. He files the paper and goes back to work. It will be thirty-three more years before he stops.
stops.quote: Thirty-three and an income of $50,000 per annum! By this time two years I can so arrange all my business as to secure at least $50,000 per annum. Beyond this never earn--make no effort to increase fortune, but spend the surplus each year for benevolent purposes... Man must have an idol--the amassing of wealth is one of the worst species of idolatry--no idol more debasing than the worship of money.
stops.quote_source: Carnegie's private memorandum, St. Nicholas Hotel, New York, December 1868, reproduced in Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), footnote 30
suggested_refs: The St. Nicholas Hotel on Broadway, where the 1868 memorandum was written
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), ed. John C. Van Dyke, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Braddock, the Edgar Thomson works blows in
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1875 as the start of production; the month is defaulted. The 1873 organisation of the partnership, with Coleman, McCandless, Stewart, Thomson and Scott among the partners, is a reconstruction from the dossier corroborated only in general terms. The coordinate is corrected to the plant's own location from a pool value about 1.7 km northwest of the footprint.
stops.campa: On the ground where Braddock's army was destroyed in 1755, the Bessemer converters light up and begin turning out steel rails. He names the works for J. Edgar Thomson, president of the Pennsylvania Railroad, which is the customer he intends to keep. The plant is built to a single doctrine: measure every cost, drive the scale up, cut the price, take the market, then reinvest the profit in a bigger plant. Partners who want dividends are bought out. Depressions are when he builds, because that is when construction is cheap.
suggested_refs: The Edgar Thomson Steel Works at Braddock, Pennsylvania, in production from 1875
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie: the steel business'

stops.name: Dunfermline, the first library
stops.date_confidence: the pool's bare '1881' is wrong for both the gift and the opening and is split here. Wikipedia's Dunfermline Carnegie Library article has plans and a gift of 8,000 pounds in 1879-80, the foundation stone laid by Margaret Carnegie on 27 July 1881, and the opening on 29 August 1883; the Andrew Carnegie article dates the gift to 1880 and Wikipedia elsewhere gives 1883 as the first Carnegie library. The date used here is the foundation stone. The coordinate is corrected about four hundred metres east of the pool's value. The Let There Be Light motto is standard on Carnegie library buildings but was not carried in the verified pool for this one.
stops.campa: He gives his birthplace a free library, the first of the more than two thousand five hundred that will carry his name, and he brings his mother from America to lay the foundation stone herself. Margaret Morrison, who borrowed twenty pounds to get the family out of this town thirty-three years ago, lays the first stone of its library while the town watches. Above the door goes the motto he uses again and again on these buildings, Let There Be Light. The library opens two years later.
suggested_refs: Dunfermline Carnegie Library, Abbot Street, foundation stone laid 27 July 1881, opened 29 August 1883

stops.name: Liverpool, the crossing with Herbert Spencer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Servia crossing with Spencer comes from Carnegie's Autobiography by way of the dossier; the month is unknown and defaulted, and the coordinate is the Liverpool Pier Head rather than a berth. Spencer's remark on visiting the Pittsburgh works is standard in the Carnegie literature but was not in the verified pool and is not independently sourced here. The 1886 publication of Triumphant Democracy is separately attested. Spencer has no journey file of his own in this collection, so nothing is inherited.
stops.campa: He sails from Liverpool with Herbert Spencer, whose books he has read as scripture and whose evolutionary account of society he takes as licence for everything he is doing in Pittsburgh: competition as a law of nature, the fittest firm surviving, charity that props up the weak as a drag on the race. He calls himself the philosopher's disciple. Spencer, taken to see the Edgar Thomson works, remarks that six months in such a place would be reason enough to want to die. Four years later Carnegie publishes Triumphant Democracy, a book of statistics arguing the American republic superior in every measurable respect to monarchical Europe.
suggested_refs: The Cunard liner Servia, on which Carnegie crossed with Herbert Spencer in 1882
Triumphant Democracy; or, Fifty Years' March of the Republic (New York and London, 1886)
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie and Herbert Spencer'
Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

segments.name: The Year of Deaths, the Marriage, the Gospel

stops.name: Cresson, typhoid and two coffins
stops.date_confidence: the two deaths are attested to the day: Thomas Morrison Carnegie of pneumonia on 19 October 1886 at Pittsburgh, Margaret Morrison Carnegie on 10 November 1886. The place of the mother's death is contradicted inside the pool, the chronology lens putting it in New York City and the geography lens at the Cresson summer residence where Andrew lay ill with typhoid. The contradiction is not resolved; the Cresson pin is used because the sickbed scene is staged there in both standard accounts consulted.
stops.campa: He is fifty and flat on his back with typhoid at the summer place in the Alleghenies when his brother Thomas, forty-three, dies of pneumonia in Pittsburgh on the nineteenth of October. Thomas ran the mills while Andrew sold bonds. Nobody tells him. Three weeks later his mother dies in the same house he is lying in, on the tenth of November, and only then is he told about his brother. He attends neither funeral. The sources disagree about where Margaret died: one puts her in New York, the rest in the room down the hall.
suggested_refs: The Carnegie summer residence at Cresson, Pennsylvania, in the autumn of 1886
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Manhattan, the Whitfield parlour
stops.date_confidence: the date and the private character of the ceremony are attested by Wikipedia and corroborated in the dossier; the exact address of the Whitfield house was not confirmed in this pass and the coordinate is a general Manhattan pin. Louise Whitfield's prenuptial agreement waiving claim on the fortune is reported in the standard accounts and is not independently checked here.
stops.campa: Four months after burying his mother he marries Louise Whitfield in her family's parlour, no crowd, no church. He is fifty-one and she is thirty; they have been attached for years and have waited on Margaret Carnegie's life. Louise signs away in advance any claim on the fortune, saying she would rather he gave it to the public than left it to her. The waiver is reported in every standard account of the marriage, and no copy of it has been produced. They are married thirty-two years and the terms are never reopened.
suggested_refs: The Whitfield family house, Manhattan, site of the private wedding of 22 April 1887
sources: Hendrick and Henderson, Louise Whitfield Carnegie (1950)

stops.name: New York, the essay called Wealth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication, North American Review, June 1889. The coordinate is his Fifth Avenue address of the period and stands for where the author lived, not for the Review's offices. The popular short form, that the man who dies rich dies disgraced, is a paraphrase; the sentence as printed is quoted here verbatim from a full-text mirror of the original essay.
stops.campa: He publishes an essay arguing that great fortunes are a trust, that leaving them to sons ruins the sons, that leaving them by will is a coward's way of giving after the giver is past caring, and that the only honourable course is to administer the surplus in one's own lifetime for the good of the community. Almsgiving he condemns outright: the money must build libraries, halls, parks, universities and baths, ladders the ambitious can climb, never doles for the improvident. Republished in Britain, it is retitled The Gospel of Wealth. What everybody quotes from it is a paraphrase; the sentence he actually printed has the word thus in it.
stops.quote: The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889, later republished as 'The Gospel of Wealth'
suggested_refs: 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889, and its British republication as 'The Gospel of Wealth'
sources: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889, full text

stops.name: Allegheny, the grant with a condition attached
stops.date_confidence: the offer is dated 1886 and the opening 1890 by the National Park Service account used here; the day and month of the opening were not established and are defaulted. The $250,000 figure is from the same source.
stops.campa: The town where he changed bobbins gets a library, a music hall and a gallery for a quarter of a million dollars, on one condition: Allegheny must tax itself to maintain the building forever. He will not endow the running costs. The capital is his and the upkeep is the public's, and a community that will not vote the maintenance does not get the gift. The clause goes into every grant afterwards, in Pittsburgh and in Dunfermline and in sixteen hundred American towns, each of which must hold a council vote before the money will move. He offers it in 1886 and the doors open in 1890.
stops.quote: There are but three modes in which surplus wealth can be disposed of. It can be left to the families of the decedents; or it can be bequeathed for public purposes; or, finally, it can be administered during their lives by its possessors.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889
suggested_refs: The Carnegie Free Library of Allegheny, Federal Street, offered 1886 and opened 1890
sources: nps.gov, 'Carnegie Libraries: The Future Made Bright, Teaching with Historic Places'

segments.name: The Dam, the Hall, and Homestead

stops.name: South Fork, the dam his club owns
stops.date_confidence: the breach between 2:50 and 2:55 pm on 31 May 1889, the death toll of 2,208, and Carnegie's membership of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club alongside Frick, Mellon, Knox and Phipps are all attested. The coordinate is corrected some 5.6 km east of the pool's value to the dam site itself. The claim that Carnegie was in Paris that day is carried by the dossier but is supported by no page reachable in this pass, and the cited National Park Service page returns 404; it is not asserted here. Where he was is simply not established.
stops.campa: Fourteen miles above Johnstown a private club of Pittsburgh steel and banking men keeps a lake for boating and fishing, held back by an old state canal dam they have lowered, screened for fish, and never properly repaired. On the afternoon of the thirty-first of May the dam gives way and twenty million tons of water go down the valley in forty minutes. Two thousand two hundred and eight people die. Carnegie is a member of the club. The club's lawyers, Knox and Reed, defeat every suit brought against it, and no member is ever held liable.
suggested_refs: The South Fork Dam and the clubhouse of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club, near St. Michael, Pennsylvania
sources: Wikipedia, 'South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club'

stops.name: Johnstown, the library after the water
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The visit of 28 November 1889 and the figure of roughly $55,000, an initial $10,000 followed by a larger gift, come from the dossier's reading of National Park Service material and were not independently reverified in this pass.
stops.campa: Six months after the flood he comes to Johnstown, walks through what is left of it, and undertakes to pay for a public library. The gift runs to about fifty-five thousand dollars, ten thousand at first and the rest afterwards. He never concedes that the club bore any responsibility for the water. Whether the building on Washington Street is a gift or a settlement is a question the town has never settled and the record does not answer. The building houses the Johnstown Flood Museum now.
suggested_refs: The Carnegie library at Johnstown, Pennsylvania, later the Johnstown Flood Museum
sources: National Park Service, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, per dossier reconstruction

stops.name: Fifty-seventh Street, the Music Hall opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The coordinate is the canonical Carnegie Hall pin already carried by several files in this collection and is reproduced here unchanged. The pool does not document Carnegie's own presence in the hall on opening night and nothing here asserts it; what is attested is that he financed the building and that Tchaikovsky took part in the inaugural festival.
stops.campa: The Music Hall he has paid for on Fifty-seventh Street, designed by William Burnet Tuthill for an acoustic rather than for a facade, opens with a five-day festival. Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, brought over for the occasion and bewildered by the size of the reception, conducts his own Marche solennelle on the first night. It keeps the name Music Hall for four more years, until the name of the man who wrote the cheque replaces the name of what the building is for. Nothing in the record places Carnegie himself in the room that evening.
suggested_refs: The Music Hall, later Carnegie Hall, 57th Street and Seventh Avenue, opened 5 May 1891
Studio 61 in the Carnegie Hall studio towers, where Martha Graham opened her school in 1926
The New York School of Expression, founded by Genevieve Stebbins inside the building in 1893
sources: Carnegie Hall, 'Five Facts About Carnegie Hall's Opening Night'
tchaikovsky.journey.json, the Carnegie Hall opening stop

stops.name: Homestead, the fence with the rifle slots
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's Homestead strike article gives 28 June 1892 for the lockout of the plate mill and an open-hearth furnace, following the expiry of the Amalgamated Association's contract amid the wage dispute. The 1892 consolidation of the partnership as the Carnegie Steel Company, with Frick as chairman and Phipps and Lauder among the partners, is separately attested. The coordinate is corrected 1.6 km east of the pool's value to the works themselves. Carnegie's written approval for contesting the union is attested; the texts of the cables are not quoted here. The fence, its rifle slots and the name Fort Frick come from Wikipedia's Homestead strike article rather than from the verified pool.
stops.campa: The interests have just been consolidated into the Carnegie Steel Company, a private partnership with Henry Clay Frick as chairman, no shareholders and nothing it must publish. The contract with the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers is running out, and Frick has already built a three-mile board fence around the plant, topped with barbed wire and drilled with slots at rifle height; the men call it Fort Frick. On the twenty-eighth of June the plate mill and an open-hearth furnace are locked out. Carnegie, who has published his sympathy for organised labour and cabled his approval for breaking this union, sails for Scotland.
suggested_refs: The board fence around the Homestead Steel Works, known as Fort Frick
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie: the strike at the Homestead mill'

stops.name: Homestead, the barges on the Monongahela
stops.date_confidence: attested. About three hundred Pinkerton agents, the attempted landing by barge before dawn, roughly ten hours of gunfire and at least ten dead, commonly given as seven workers or their supporters and three Pinkertons, all from Wikipedia's Homestead strike article. Counts of the dead vary slightly between accounts and are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: Before dawn two barges are towed up the Monongahela carrying about three hundred armed Pinkerton agents, hired to put the plant back in company hands. The town is awake and waiting on the bank. The shooting starts at the landing and goes on for some ten hours, with the strikers firing from behind steel billets and pumping oil onto the river to burn the barges. At least ten men are killed. In the afternoon the Pinkertons surrender their arms and are marched through the town, and the crowd beats them the length of the street.
suggested_refs: The Pinkerton landing site on the Monongahela at the Homestead works, 6 July 1892
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie: the strike at the Homestead mill'

stops.name: Loch Rannoch, inaccessible to all
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was at a rented castle on Loch Rannoch in Perthshire during the crisis and reachable only by cable, per the PBS American Experience account. The exact day is an ordering device set two days after the battle, consistent with his own statement that news reached him two days after the strike began. The quoted sentences were written years later for the Autobiography and are a retrospective judgement, not a contemporary reaction.
stops.campa: He is in the Highlands, in a rented castle on a loch, and the cables reach him there within two days. Reporters come north and are turned away. Workers who try to get word to the owner over the head of his chairman find there is no road to him. He does not come back. He does not repudiate Frick, and he does not order the plant reopened on the old terms; from Scotland he cables Frick his support. The British radical press, which has printed him for twenty years as the friend of the working man, turns on him inside a fortnight.
stops.quote: No pangs remain of any wound received in my business career save that of Homestead. It was so unnecessary. The men were outrageously wrong.
stops.quote_source: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), chapter XVII, 'The Homestead Strike'
suggested_refs: The rented castle on Loch Rannoch, Perthshire, occupied during the Homestead crisis
sources: pbs.org, American Experience, 'Carnegie: the strike at the Homestead mill'
Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), chapter XVII, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: Homestead, the militia and the vote to go back
stops.date_confidence: attested. Governor Robert E. Pattison's militia of roughly 8,500 arrives 12 July; Alexander Berkman shoots and stabs Frick in his Pittsburgh office on 23 July and Frick survives; the Homestead lodge votes 101 to 91 to return on 20 November. Wikipedia dates the strike 1 July to 20 November and gives 143 days, correcting the pool's 144. Berkman acts alone and has no connection to the union, which the press ignores.
stops.campa: Governor Pattison sends eight and a half thousand state troops, who take the hills above the town in the second week of July and hold the mill open for replacement workers. On the twenty-third an anarchist named Alexander Berkman walks into Frick's Pittsburgh office and shoots him twice and stabs him; Frick finishes the day's work before letting a surgeon in. The lockout runs a hundred and forty-three days. On the twentieth of November the lodge votes a hundred and one to ninety-one to go back on the company's terms. Unionism is finished in American steel for the next forty years.
stops.quote: Kind master, tell us what you wish us to do and we shall do it for you.
stops.quote_source: Cable from officers of the Carnegie workmen to Andrew Carnegie, 1892, quoted in Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), chapter XVII, as having arrived too late
suggested_refs: The militia encampment on the hills above Homestead, July 1892
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), chapter XVII, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

segments.name: Skibo, the Sale, and the Rectorship

stops.name: Skibo Castle, the Scottish half of the year
stops.date_confidence: leased 1897 and bought 1898 per the Carnegie Club's own history; the month is defaulted. The coordinate is corrected some 8.8 km south of the pool's value to the castle itself. Margaret Carnegie, the only child, is born in 1897, which is the stated reason for wanting a permanent Scottish house. The piper, the organist and the guest list are Skibo tradition carried by the estate's own history rather than by any document read in this pass, and no individual guest is named here.
stops.campa: A daughter is born to him at sixty-one and he wants a house in Scotland to raise her in, so he leases a Sutherland estate on the Dornoch Firth, buys it the year after, and rebuilds it into something between a castle and a hotel. He spends half of every year here, an ocean from the mills, running the largest steel company on earth by cable. A piper wakes the house each morning and walks the terrace under the windows. An organist plays him down to breakfast. The guest book, which the estate still keeps, runs to writers, pianists, cabinet ministers, financiers and a king.
suggested_refs: Skibo Castle, Sutherland, leased 1897 and purchased 1898

stops.name: Skibo, the pencil note about McLuckie
stops.date_confidence: the pencil note is verbatim from Carnegie's own Autobiography, chapter XVII. The dating is an ordering device: the meeting with McLuckie in Mexico is narrated by John C. Van Dyke, the book's editor, who places the first encounter in the spring of 1900 and the remark at a later meeting, about 1900 or 1901, at the railway shops at Guaymas, Sonora. The pool's dating of 1893 and its description of the account as a letter from a mutual acquaintance are both wrong and are corrected here. Carnegie's own pin is used; he never went to Sonora.
stops.campa: John McLuckie was burgess of Homestead and one of the leaders of the strike, and afterwards he was blacklisted out of the trade, lost his wife, and drifted to Mexico. Van Dyke finds him there penniless and writes to Carnegie, who scrawls his answer in pencil in the margin. By the time the offer reaches him McLuckie has found work in the railway shops at Guaymas and will not take the money, but he asks who sent it. Told it was Carnegie, he says: Well, that was damned white of Andy, wasn't it?
stops.quote: Give McLuckie all the money he wants, but don't mention my name.
stops.quote_source: Carnegie's pencilled note on a letter concerning John McLuckie, quoted in Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), chapter XVII
suggested_refs: John C. Van Dyke's inset first-person narrative of meeting John McLuckie in Sonora, Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie, chapter XVII
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), ed. John C. Van Dyke, chapter XVII, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: New York, the company sold in a morning
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia gives the completion of the transaction and the figure of roughly $225.64 million to Carnegie personally in gold bonds, with the whole of United States Steel capitalised far higher. The famous exchange of a written price on a slip of paper is a widely repeated account and is not independently verified in this pass. J. P. Morgan has no journey file here yet, so nothing is inherited.
stops.campa: J. P. Morgan buys the Carnegie Steel Company and folds it into the United States Steel Corporation, the first billion-dollar company in the world. Carnegie's own share comes to some two hundred and twenty-five million dollars in fifty-year gold bonds; he requires bonds because he will not hold stock in anything he is not running. He is sixty-five. At thirty-three he had written himself a plan to be out of business by thirty-five and to give the surplus away. He is thirty years late, and the surplus is four thousand times the sum he had in mind when he wrote it.
suggested_refs: The 1901 sale of Carnegie Steel to the United States Steel Corporation, in fifty-year five percent gold bonds

stops.name: Washington, an institution for research and not for teaching
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, 29 January 1902, with an initial endowment of $10 million later raised to about $22 million. The Eugenics Record Office relation is a funding relation, not a visit: Carnegie is named in this collection's alexander_graham_bell and prescott_bush files as one of three money streams behind the office at Cold Spring Harbor, founded 1910, whose Board of Scientific Directors Bell chaired from about 1910 to 1918. Whether Carnegie personally directed any of it is not established, and no stop is staged at Cold Spring Harbor, where he never went.
stops.campa: He endows an institution in Washington with ten million dollars, later more than doubled, on a principle he keeps repeating: it is to pay for original investigation, not for classrooms. Astronomy, terrestrial magnetism, plant biology, embryology. Among the things his institution's money reaches is the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, founded in 1910 on Harriman, Rockefeller and Carnegie funds, whose Board of Scientific Directors is chaired by Alexander Graham Bell, and which spends two decades collecting family pedigrees and grading American bloodlines.
suggested_refs: The Carnegie Institution of Washington, 1530 P Street NW, founded 29 January 1902
The Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, funded in part from Carnegie money
sources: alexander_graham_bell.journey.json, the Eugenics Record Office stop

stops.name: Ninety-first Street, sixty-four rooms
stops.date_confidence: the house is built 1899-1902 and the family moves in about the end of 1902; the day is defaulted. The sixty-four rooms, the central heating, the elevator and the later naming of Carnegie Hill are attested; the purchase of surrounding lots to protect the light is house tradition and was not in the verified pool. The quoted sentence is from the 1889 essay and is set against the house deliberately: the juxtaposition is the file's, not the source's.
stops.campa: The house he builds on what is then the northern edge of fashionable New York has sixty-four rooms, its own steam heating plant, a passenger elevator, a pipe organ and a private garden. He buys the surrounding lots so that nobody can build over the light, though that last is house tradition rather than deed. The neighbourhood takes the name Carnegie Hill. Thirteen years earlier he had written that the first duty of a man of wealth is to set an example of modest and unostentatious living. He appears to have meant it. Against what, or against whom, he was measuring modest is not a thing he ever set down.
stops.quote: First, to set an example of modest, unostentatious living, shunning display or extravagance
stops.quote_source: Andrew Carnegie, 'Wealth,' North American Review, June 1889
suggested_refs: The Andrew Carnegie Mansion, 2 East 91st Street, now the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum

stops.name: Pittencrieff, the glen bought and handed over
stops.date_confidence: the purchase and conveyance are dated 1902-1903 by the Carnegie Corporation's own account; the day and month are defaulted. The statue erected on the park's northern boundary in 1914 is attested by Wikipedia's Pittencrieff Park article, which gives no unveiling date and does not place Carnegie there; it is folded into this stop rather than given a scene of its own.
stops.campa: He buys the walled glen his family was not allowed to enter and gives it to Dunfermline outright, with a trust to pay for its upkeep and for concerts, baths, gardens and lectures in the town. The gates come off. He says afterwards that this gave him more pleasure than any hall or institution or endowment he ever paid for, the boy who was kept out and the man who bought the wall being the same person. In 1914 the town puts up a statue of him on the park's northern edge, facing the Abbey where the Bruce lies, a quarter of a mile from the room where his father worked the loom. No unveiling date is recorded and nothing places him at it.
suggested_refs: Pittencrieff Park, Dunfermline, purchased 1902-1903 and conveyed to the town
The Carnegie statue on the northern boundary of Pittencrieff Park, erected 1914

stops.name: St Andrews, the rector's second address
stops.date_confidence: the pool's '1903, 1905' for the elections is wrong and is corrected: Carnegie was Rector of the University of St Andrews from 1901 to 1907, elected 1901 and re-elected 1904, per Wikipedia's list of rectors. 1905 is the year of the second rectorial address, published in 1906 as 'A League of Peace'; the day and month are defaulted.
stops.campa: The university elects him rector in 1901 and again in 1904, and the city of St Andrews gives him its freedom. He uses the second rectorial address to argue for something that does not yet exist: a league of the strongest nations, bound to submit their quarrels to arbitration and to hold the peace by their combined weight against any state that will not. He is sixty-nine, and rector until 1907. The address goes to the printer and comes back the following year under the title A League of Peace.
suggested_refs: 'A League of Peace,' the rectorial address delivered at St Andrews in 1905 and published in 1906
sources: university-collections.wp.st-andrews.ac.uk, 'Philanthropist Andrew Carnegie and the University of St Andrews'
Wikipedia, 'Rector of the University of St Andrews'

stops.name: Tuskegee, the library and the steel securities
stops.date_confidence: the 1906 visit is attested by the Carnegie Birthplace Museum's account, as is the arc of the relationship: an unsuccessful solicitation by Booker T. Washington in 1890, about $20,000 for a library by 1900, and a later gift of United States Steel securities reported at about $600,000. Day and month are defaulted; the $600,000 figure is a reported one and is not independently verified. The Edinburgh address of 16 October 1907 is attested by the pamphlet's publication record, but the Philosophical Institution's building was not confirmed and no separate stop is staged for it.
stops.campa: Booker T. Washington asks him for money in 1890 and is refused. Ten years later he gets twenty thousand dollars for a library, which the students build themselves out of bricks they make on the ground. In 1906 Carnegie comes to Alabama to see the institute, and afterwards settles on it United States Steel securities reported at some six hundred thousand dollars, part of it in trust for Washington personally so the man would stop having to raise his own salary. The following autumn, before the Philosophical Institution of Edinburgh, he lectures a Scottish audience on the condition of Black Americans and prints it as a pamphlet.
suggested_refs: The Carnegie Library at Tuskegee Institute, built by students from bricks they made themselves
The Negro in America: An Address Delivered before the Philosophical Institution of Edinburgh (1907)
sources: carnegiebirthplace.com, 'Andrew Carnegie and Booker T. Washington'
Publication record, The Negro in America, Edinburgh, 1907

segments.name: The Peace That Does Not Come, and the Last House

stops.name: New York, the Endowment for International Peace
stops.date_confidence: the pool paired 'on his seventy-fifth birthday' with 14 December 1910, which is false and is corrected here. His seventy-fifth birthday was 25 November 1910 and that is when he announced the Endowment; the formal deed of gift of $10 million in first-mortgage five percent bonds was presented on 14 December 1910, which is the official establishment date and the one used. The coordinate is his own house, not the Endowment's later offices. The instruction to the trustees to move on to the next greatest evil once war is abolished is the standard account of the deed's language; the deed itself was not read in this pass.
stops.campa: He gives ten million dollars in first-mortgage bonds to a board of trustees with an instruction that has embarrassed every trustee since: abolish international war, and when that is done, meet again and decide what the next greatest evil is and turn the money on that. He announces it on his seventy-fifth birthday, the twenty-fifth of November, and signs the deed of gift three weeks later. He is not being decorative about the timetable. He believes in 1910 that war between the great states is nearly finished and that the money will outlive the problem.
suggested_refs: The deed of gift of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 14 December 1910

stops.name: New York, the Corporation that holds the rest
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1911; the day and month are defaulted. carnegie.org gives an endowment of $135 million at founding, while the editorial footnote in the Autobiography that carries the quoted object refers to a gift of $125,000,000; the two figures are not reconciled here. The quoted text is Carnegie's own statement of purpose to the trustees.
stops.campa: He is seventy-six and giving the money away is not going fast enough, so he stops trying to do it personally and creates a corporation to do it after him, handing over the bulk of what is left. The letter to the trustees sets the object in a single sentence and then leaves them the widest discretion it can, in the words agencies and means as shall from time to time be found appropriate. The size of the founding endowment is given two ways in the record: a hundred and thirty-five million dollars by the institution itself, a hundred and twenty-five million in the footnote to his own book.
stops.quote: To promote the advancement and diffusion of knowledge and understanding among the people of the United States by aiding technical schools, institutions of higher learning, libraries, scientific research, hero funds, useful publications and by such other agencies and means as shall from time to time be found appropriate therefor.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Carnegie, letter to the trustees of the Carnegie Corporation of New York, 1911, quoted in Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), footnote 61
suggested_refs: The 1911 letter of gift establishing the Carnegie Corporation of New York
sources: Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), footnote 61, Project Gutenberg ebook 17976

stops.name: La Plata, the dinosaur with his name on it
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the La Plata installation, from the Spanish Wikipedia article on the Museo de La Plata: the cast set up in 1912 by the Carnegie Museum's director William J. Holland, who travelled to Argentina to assemble it. Carnegie never went to Argentina and the stop is for the object he paid for and gave, not for a visit; Holland's journey is Holland's. The type specimen CM 84 from Sheep Creek, Wyoming, 1899, and the naming by John Bell Hatcher in 1901, are attested; the per-city years for the casts come from the Carnegie Museums Magazine and Wikipedia gives only a distribution window of 1905 to 1928.
stops.campa: A near-complete sauropod comes out of Sheep Creek, Wyoming, in 1899, dug by an expedition he paid for, and John Bell Hatcher names it Diplodocus carnegii. He has plaster casts made and sends them to heads of state: London, Berlin, Paris, Vienna, Bologna, St. Petersburg, Madrid, Mexico City. One crosses the equator: William Holland, who runs the Carnegie Museum, comes down from Pittsburgh in 1912 to put it together himself in the hall of the Museo de La Plata, in the province of Buenos Aires, where it still stands under a steelmaker's surname. The London cast is touring Britain a century later. Carnegie never sees either of them in place.
suggested_refs: The Diplodocus carnegii cast at the Museo de La Plata, Buenos Aires province, installed 1912
The Diplodocus carnegii cast at the Natural History Museum, London, presented 1905 and toured Britain 2018 to 2020
sources: Carnegie Museums Magazine, 'The Dinosaur That Changed the World'

stops.name: The Hague, the Peace Palace opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the opening. The coordinate is the canonical Peace Palace pin already carried by other files in this collection and is reproduced unchanged; the pool's geography lens gave a value some seven hundred metres southwest, which is rejected. The gift of $1.5 million, secured through Andrew Dickson White, is dated 1903. The quoted phrase is Carnegie on the coming of peace, carried by the Peace Palace record.
stops.campa: He puts up a million and a half dollars for a temple of peace at The Hague to house the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and insists the Dutch government take formal responsibility for it so that it is a public building and not a rich man's monument. It opens on the twenty-eighth of August, 1913. Eleven months later Europe is at war, and the court in the new building has no case before it that anybody intends to submit. A bust of the donor stands inside.
stops.quote: as certain to come, and come soon, as day follows night
stops.quote_source: Andrew Carnegie on the coming of international peace, cited in the Peace Palace record
suggested_refs: The Peace Palace on the Carnegieplein, The Hague, opened 28 August 1913, seat of the Permanent Court of Arbitration

stops.name: New York, before the Commission on Industrial Relations
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the printed reprint of the testimony, 'Mr. Carnegie's Testimony Before the United States Commission on Industrial Relations, February 5th, 1915,' reprinted from the New York Herald. The hearing room's address was not established and the coordinate is lower Manhattan generally.
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after Homestead, at seventy-nine, he is called before federal investigators looking into the relations of labour and capital in America. He tells them his own principles always favoured consultation, arbitration and the workmen's right to organise, and that what happened at Homestead happened while he was abroad. The commissioners have the cables in front of them. The war in Europe is six months old. He never appears again in public to any consequence, and the manuscript of the autobiography, broken off the year before, is never taken up again.
suggested_refs: Mr. Carnegie's Testimony Before the United States Commission on Industrial Relations, February 5th, 1915
sources: Mr. Carnegie's Testimony Before the United States Commission on Industrial Relations, reprinted from the New York Herald

stops.name: Lenox, the last summer at Shadowbrook
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the death, bronchial pneumonia following influenza and earlier attacks of pneumonia, per contemporaneous obituary notices and Louise Carnegie's 1920 preface to the Autobiography. The marriage of Margaret Carnegie to Roswell Miller Jr. at the New York mansion on 22 April 1919 is attested by the dossier's family section and is folded in here. The coordinate is corrected some seven kilometres west of the pool's value to the Shadowbrook estate site, now the Kripalu Center; Wikipedia places it in Stockbridge while noting it is often described as being in Lenox. The mansion burned in 1956.
stops.campa: In April he gives his only daughter away at the house on Ninety-first Street, on the same date of the year he married Louise thirty-two years before. Then the Berkshires. The estate is the last house he buys, taken in 1917 when the crossings stop and Skibo becomes unreachable. He has not written a line of the autobiography since the war began; the manuscript stops in 1914, and his wife will say in the preface that the light went out of him then. He dies there on the morning of the eleventh of August, of bronchial pneumonia, at eighty-three, having given away some three hundred and fifty million dollars.
suggested_refs: Shadowbrook, Lenox and Stockbridge, Massachusetts, the last Carnegie residence, burned 1956
sources: Louise Whitfield Carnegie's 1920 preface to the Autobiography

stops.name: Sleepy Hollow, the stone quarried at Skibo
stops.date_confidence: the burial is attested to August 1919; the exact day of interment was not established and the fourteenth is used as an ordering value. The coordinate is the cemetery's own and corrects a pool value about 1.15 km to the south-southwest. The Celtic-cross form, the Skibo granite and the sculptor George Henry Paulin are attested. That Samuel Gompers lies a short distance away is not supported by the cited source, which lists both men among notable burials and says nothing about the plots; only the shared cemetery is claimed here.
stops.campa: He is buried in a Westchester cemetery under a granite Celtic cross, cut by George Henry Paulin in Glasgow from stone quarried on his own Sutherland estate and shipped across the Atlantic, which is as close as he comes to being buried in Scotland. He had asked for nothing elaborate and the cross is plain, with the dates and the two countries on it. In the same ground lies Samuel Gompers, who led the American Federation of Labor through the years when the union at Homestead was broken. Louise outlives her husband by twenty-seven years, their daughter Margaret until 1990. Visitors leave coins on the stone.
suggested_refs: The Carnegie grave at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, a Celtic cross of Skibo granite carved by George Henry Paulin

stops.name: New York, the Corporation takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: carnegie.org's own news feed carries 'Carnegie Corporation of New York Changes Its Name to the Andrew Carnegie Foundation,' dated 9 June 2026, and the new name is live on the institution's site. The coordinate is the Carnegie mansion on Ninety-first Street, used as his own pin; the foundation's offices are elsewhere in Manhattan.
stops.campa: A hundred and fifteen years after the letter to the trustees, the Carnegie Corporation of New York renames itself the Andrew Carnegie Foundation. The institution he built to outlive him, and to spend his money on objects he could not name in advance, now carries the one thing he had once asked to be kept out of a gift: his name. Some sixteen hundred and eighty-nine of his libraries were built in the United States and about two thousand five hundred in all, in Scotland and Ireland and Canada and New Zealand and South Africa. The announcement is dated the ninth of June, 2026.
suggested_refs: carnegie.org, 'Carnegie Corporation of New York Changes Its Name to the Andrew Carnegie Foundation,' 9 June 2026
